IT 105 — DISCRETE STRUCTURES 1

2nd Semester — Prelim — Week 1

PRELIM — WEEK 1

1. PROPOSITIONAL LOGIC

What is Propositional Logic?

Propositional logic, also known as sentential logic and statement logic, is the branch of logic that studies ways of combining or modifying entire propositions, statements or sentences to form more complicated propositions, statements or sentences, as well as the logical relationships and properties.

2. DISCRETE MATHEMATICS

What is Discrete Mathematics?

Discrete Mathematics deals with mathematical objects that can be enumerated or logically structured, such as:

• Integers
• Sets
• Logical statements
• Functions
• Algorithm
• Graphs
• Combinatorics
• etc.

2. DISCRETE MATHEMATICS

Definition

Discrete Mathematics is the branch of mathematics that studies structures that are distinct and countable, rather than continuous.

Discrete means non-continuous:

“distinct, or not connected”.

DISCRETE VS. CONTINUOUS

DISCRETE
The number of pennies in your pocket.

CONTINUOUS
The time measured in minutes.
The height of students in a class.
The temperature measured in degrees Celsius.
The length of a rope measured in meters.

3. LOGIC

What is Logic?

Logic is the study of formal mathematics, the foundation of mathematical reasoning and proofs itself.

In discrete mathematics, it provides tools for analyzing:

• Statements
• Arguments
• Proofs
• Examples

The source gives these examples:
“2 + 2 = 4”
“The sky is green.”

4. PROPOSITIONS

Definition of a Proposition

A proposition is a declarative statement that is either true or false.

Examples

Example 1
“2 + 2 = 4” → TRUE

Example 2
“The sky is green.” → FALSE

Example 3
“Go home.” → Not a proposition: command

Example 4
“Are you okay?” → Not a proposition: question

4. PROPOSITIONS

Key Idea

For a statement to be a proposition, it must be a declarative statement that has a truth value:

true or false.

5. LOGICAL CONNECTIVES

Definition

A logical connective is a symbol which is used to connect two or more propositional or predicate logics in such a manner that resultant logic depends only on the input logics and the meaning of the connective used.

Logical Connective     Symbol
Conjunction                 ∧
Disjunction                 ∨
Exclusive OR                ⊕
Implication                 ⇒
Biconditional               ↔

The source then explains each connective individually.

6. NEGATION

Definition
Negation reverses the truth value of a proposition.

Meaning: NOT p
Symbols: ¬p or ~p

Suppose p is a proposition.
The negation of p is: ~p
The meaning of ~p: p is false.

Negation Examples

Example 1
p: “It is raining.”
Therefore: ~p: “It is not raining.”

Example 2
p: “I will not study.”
Therefore: ~p: “I will study.”

6. NEGATION

Core Rule

Negation changes the truth value of a proposition.

If:
p = TRUE
then:
~p = FALSE

And if:
p = FALSE
then:
~p = TRUE

7. CONJUNCTION

Definition
A conjunction is TRUE only when BOTH statements are true.

Meaning: AND
Symbol: ∧

Suppose p, q are propositions.

Example
p: The sky is blue.
q: The grass is green.

Therefore:
p ∧ q = The sky is blue and the grass is green.

The source also labels the logical structure with:
• premises
• conclusion

Core Rule
For p ∧ q, the result is TRUE only when p is TRUE and q is TRUE.

Both statements must be true.

8. DISJUNCTION

Definition
A disjunction is FALSE only when BOTH statements are false.

Meaning: OR
Symbol: ∨

Suppose p, q are propositions.

Example
p: It is raining.
q: It is snowing.

Therefore:
p ∨ q = It is raining or it is snowing.

Core Rule
For p ∨ q, the result is FALSE only when p is FALSE and q is FALSE.

If at least one of the two statements is TRUE, the disjunction is TRUE.

9. EXCLUSIVE OR

Definition
Exclusive OR is TRUE if exactly one is true.

Meaning: Exclusive OR (XOR)
Symbol: ⊕

Suppose p, q are propositions.

Example
p: I will eat burger.
q: I will eat fries.

Therefore:
p ⊕ q = I will eat either burger or fries.

NOT both at the same time.

9. EXCLUSIVE OR

Core Rule

For p ⊕ q, exactly one proposition must be TRUE.

Therefore:
p = TRUE, q = FALSE → TRUE
p = FALSE, q = TRUE → TRUE
p = TRUE, q = TRUE → FALSE
p = FALSE, q = FALSE → FALSE

The important distinction presented by the source is:

NOT both at the same time

10. CONDITIONAL / IMPLICATION

Conditional (Implication)

A conditional, or implication, is FALSE only when p is TRUE and q is FALSE.

Meaning: Implies (IF… THEN)
Symbol: ⇒

Suppose p, q are propositions.

Example
p: I study.
q: I pass.

Therefore:
p ⇒ q = If I study, then I pass.

Important Note
In implication there is always IF… THEN in conclusion.

Core Rule
For p ⇒ q, the implication is FALSE only when p = TRUE and q = FALSE.

All other combinations result in TRUE.

11. BICONDITIONAL

Biconditional (If and only if)

A biconditional is TRUE when both values are the same.

Meaning: Equivalence (If and only if)
Symbol: ↔

Suppose p, q are propositions.

Example
p: You can access the system.
q: You have a password.

Therefore, the source gives:
p ⇒ q = You can access the system if and only if you have a password.

11. BICONDITIONAL

Important Source Note

The source's displayed formula uses p ⇒ q in this example even though the section identifies the biconditional symbol as ↔.

Core Rule

For p ↔ q, the result is TRUE when both truth values are the same:

p = TRUE, q = TRUE → TRUE
p = FALSE, q = FALSE → TRUE

It is FALSE when their truth values are different.

12. CONNECTIVE REFERENCE

NEGATION
Meaning: NOT p
Symbol: ¬p / ~p
Main Rule: Reverses the truth value

CONJUNCTION
Meaning: AND
Symbol: ∧
Main Rule: TRUE only when BOTH statements are true

DISJUNCTION
Meaning: OR
Symbol: ∨
Main Rule: FALSE only when BOTH statements are false

12. CONNECTIVE REFERENCE

EXCLUSIVE OR
Meaning: Exclusive OR (XOR)
Symbol: ⊕
Main Rule: TRUE if exactly one is true

CONDITIONAL / IMPLICATION
Meaning: Implies (IF… THEN)
Symbol: ⇒
Main Rule: FALSE only when p is TRUE and q is FALSE

BICONDITIONAL
Meaning: Equivalence (If and only if)
Symbol: ↔
Main Rule: TRUE when both values are the same
